description_full: Weyerhaeuser Company is the world's largest private owners of timberlands and today owns or controls more than 10 million acres of timberlands in the U.S., as well as additional public timberlands managed under long-term licenses in Canada. Weyerhaeuser has been a global leader in sustainability for more than a century and manages 100 percent of its timberlands on a fully sustainable basis in compliance with internationally recognized sustainable forestry standards. Weyerhaeuser is also one of the largest manufacturers of wood products in North America and operates additional business lines around product distribution, climate solutions, real estate, energy and natural resources, among others. In 2025, the company generated 6.9 billion dollar in net sales and employed approximately 9,500 people who serve customers worldwide. Weyerhaeuser Company was founded in 1900 and was incorporated in Washington.
ceo_bio: Mr. Devin W. Stockfish Esq., J.D. | President, CEO & Director | Age 51 | Compensation: $3.4M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 9K people. Revenue per employee of $727K ranks in the bottom quartile among Real Estate peers. Each employee generates $54K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $5K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 5× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (1/10).
financial_summary: Weyerhaeuser Company is a large-cap real estate business with a $15.0B market cap on $6.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -12% over the past three years and -0% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.

Returns on capital run at 7% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 22% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $511M in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.73× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 4.1× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 2.7× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 5.1% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 11% operating margin trails the Real Estate median (23%) by 12pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.

growth: Revenue has compounded at -12.1% over 3 years, -1.7% over 5 years and -0.3% over 10 years, so the decline is deepening, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 15%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -19.1% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: deferred revenue up 20% and FFO growth of -18.1% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.1x depreciation (0.7% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.3%), and institutions hold 93%.

It returns 5.1% a year to shareholders (1.1% in buybacks and 4.0% in dividends).
